extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, fiction writers, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and applying a narrative method (dramatic/scene-based vs. pictorial/narratorial), assigning point of view, and using showing/telling and background to best serve a novel's subject and scale. Emphasises when a narrator is needed and when the story should be entrusted to the characters' action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer direct view unless narrator adds value
rubrics_metrics.description: "Unless the presence of a seer and a recorder is made a value in itself, contributing definitely to the effect of the subject, he is better dispensed with and put out of the way; where other things are equal a direct view of the matter in hand is the best."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a direct dramatised presentation (scenes, speech, visible action) when it will convey the subject fully. Retain an explicit narrator only if that narrator's voice/stance contributes a necessary effect or economy to the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator as principle of economy and value
rubrics_metrics.description: "The narrator... represents the great principle of economy, and is a value in himself, and does contribute to the effect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subject calls for panoramic summarizing, broad generalization, or economy of presentation over large scope, an authorial narrator can be an asset—use the narrator deliberately to picture and summarize where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a dramatic subject
rubrics_metrics.description: A dramatic subject is "a clean-cut situation, raising the question of its issue, and by answering the question the subject is treated. What will these people do, how will they circumvent this awkwardness? That is what the book is to show — action essentially, not the puzzle of character or a state behind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the core of the story is an action or problem resolvable by visible behaviour across a small, contained circle or sequence of scenes, treat it scenically (drama). Example: The Awkward Age (Nanda's manipulation of elders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a pictorial/panoramic subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Large, loose, manifold subjects "extensive in time and space, full of crowds and diversions," are "a pictorial subject and can be nothing else," requiring the narrator's survey and summaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For stories that cover long spans of time, many locations, or large social panoramas, rely on an authorial viewpoint/narrator to compress, generalize, and orient the reader (examples: Thackeray's chronicles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale/amount determines method
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is simply a question of amount, of quantity, of the reach of the subject. If it passes a certain point it exceeds the capacity of the straight and dramatic method."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose dramatic (scene-based) method when subject scope is limited; choose pictorial/narratorial method when scope is large. Evaluate subject reach before committing to a single method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show internal life through gestures and looks
rubrics_metrics.description: "The story that is concerned... with the impact of experience upon a mind... can be enhanced to the pitch of drama, because thought has its tell-tale gestures and its speaking looks... Make use of these looks and gestures, express the story through them, leave them to enact it — and you have a story which in its manner is effectually drama."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To dramatize internal states, convert thoughts into observable signs (gestures, looks, small actions) rather than explicit interior exposition. Let readers infer inner life from external behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let scenes embody implications rather than explicit announcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Example passage: "The thought is between him and the good woman as they talk; the dialogue, with its allusions and broken phrases, slowly shapes itself to the form of the suppressed appeal... The scene has embodied it; the cheerless little room... have all contributed; the broken phrases, without touching it, have travelled about it and revealed its contour."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey emotional appeals, moral implications, and motives by arranging setting, dialogue, action and fragmentary speech so the significance emerges organically, instead of stating it outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain methodical consistency when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: The author may choose to render a story "with absolute consistency, on one method only" (e.g., The Awkward Age is pure drama throughout).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you commit to a strict method (pure drama or pure pictorial/subjective narration), maintain that method to preserve unity and strength of effect. Beware mixing methods without clear artistic justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed method is legitimate when justified
rubrics_metrics.description: "When it is time to suggest that even in dealing with a subject entirely dramatic, a novelist may well find reason to keep to his old familiar mixed method — circumspice: it would appear that he does so invariably."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend scene-based drama and authorial summary when the subject needs both close action and wider context; ensure each intrudes only when it serves a concrete purpose (background, memory, generalization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic method is powerful but limited in background depth
rubrics_metrics.description: "The play-form... is hampered in its power to express the outlying associations of its scene... From the point of view of the reader... the dramatic scene is vivid and compact; but it is narrow, it can have no great depth, and the colour of the atmosphere can hardly tell within the space."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the story's effect depends on setting, social texture, or pervasive atmosphere, supplement strict drama with descriptive or narratorial devices to supply background without flattening the immediate action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pictorial/setting work to propel drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Balzac example: thorough preparation of setting (Maison Vauquer) supplies "character and energy for the drama when it begins," making the background a "propulsive force applied to the action at the start."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When background materially fuels characters' motives or the action, invest time in creating rich, economical pictorial description so that later scenes inherit that energy and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid authorial convenience that embarrasses the story
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is an easy-going reliance on a narrator... He seems to come forward in many a case without doing the story any particular service; sometimes he actually embarrasses it, when a matter of vivid drama is violently forced into the form of a narration."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use omniscient narration merely for authorial ease. If narration is used to cover weaknesses in dramatization, it may weaken rather than help the story; prefer strengthening scenes instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare and approach turns of events deliberately (undercutting flat impressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of undercutting: "wherever a turn of events is carefully prepared and deliberately approached" the flat impression is undercut and the drama gains pictorial relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreshadow and stage dramatic turns so they feel both inevitable and surprising; craft scenes and details that accumulate toward the revelation rather than dumping it abruptly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelist's control over speech and manner (amplified stage-direction)
rubrics_metrics.description: In The Awkward Age "whatever is not dialogue is simply a kind of amplified stage-direction, adding to the dialogue the expressive effect which might be given it by good acting. The novelist... creates the manner in which the words are spoken, as well as the words themselves..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting a dramatic method, control not only dialogue but also the reported manner (tone, timing, pauses, gestures) so the reader experiences an 'ideal' performance rather than relying on external interpretation.
